titre: Iceland's Althing: A Law That Lived in One Memory
accroche: Starting in 930, Iceland elected a man for three years with a single task: reciting a third of the law from memory each summer, for lack of a written text.
contenu_vulgarise:
Every summer, free Icelanders gathered at Þingvellir for the Althing, the general assembly founded in 930. One man stood on the Lögberg, the Law Rock, and recited aloud a third of the rules that governed the country. No one in the crowd held a written copy to check him against: at that moment, Icelandic law existed nowhere else but in his memory.

## One office, one function

This man was the lögsögumaður, literally the "law-speaker." The Lögrétta, the assembly's legislative council, elected him for a three-year term. His task, according to a Library of Congress blog post on Þingvellir, was to memorize Icelandic law and recite it over that period. Grágás, the Icelandic law code, specifies that the whole body of law had to be covered in three summers, a third each year, before the holder gave up the office. It was, per the same post, the only paid position in the entire Icelandic Commonwealth: no king, no central administration ran the island, and the pay was the price of a skill no one else held to the same degree.

Tradition, reported by the medieval historian Ari Þorgilsson and relayed by Wikipedia, credits a man named Úlfljótr with introducing Iceland's first laws in the 920s, modeled on Norwegian law. Úlfljótr was not yet a lawspeaker in the full sense: the office itself was born with the Althing, in 930. Holding the role required a voice that carried as much as a reliable memory. Wikipedia reports that one of the earliest holders, Grímr Svertingsson, had his term cut short because his voice was too weak for the task.

## What memory never quite replaces

As long as the law was recited only once a year, by one man, in one place, it stayed vulnerable to forgetting, error, and disputes that no written page could settle. In 1117, the Althing decided for the first time to set down the entire body of law in writing. According to Wikipedia's article on Grágás, the text was drafted the following winter, at Hafliði Másson's farm, and made public the next year, in 1118. This shift did not end the office of lawspeaker, which survived until the Althing itself was abolished in 1800, but it changed its nature: the holder was no longer the sole living version of the law; he now presided over and recited something that also existed on parchment and could be reread without him.

The Grágás that has come down to us is not, in fact, that 1117-1118 manuscript, long lost, but two later copies, Konungsbók (around 1260) and Staðarhólsbók (around 1280), themselves written after Iceland had come under the Norwegian crown and adopted a different body of law. Putting the law in writing did not fix Icelandic law once and for all: it only changed the nature of the risk. Before 1117, a badly recited law was lost along with its speaker. Afterward, it could be lost with the parchment, or survive, distorted, in a copy of a copy.

repere.texte: The lögsögumaður was the only paid office in the entire Icelandic Commonwealth, according to a Library of Congress blog post on the assembly at Þingvellir.
repere.source: Library of Congress, In Custodia Legis blog, "Þingvellir: Northern Europe's First Parliament," 2016

carte.punch: In 930, Iceland founded its parliament but entrusted its law to one man's memory.
carte.idee: At Iceland's Althing, founded in 930, an elected lawspeaker (lögsögumaður) served a three-year term with one task: memorize the law and recite a third of it each summer, standing on the Lögberg. Not until 1117 did the assembly decide, for the first time, to write it down.

quiz.question: Why did Iceland's Althing, starting in 930, elect a lawspeaker for a three-year term?
choix: To have him memorize the law and recite a third of it each summer, for lack of a written text
To have him alone judge disputes between farmers, in place of the Lögrétta
To have him command the assembly's expeditions in case of conflict
To have him collect the dues owed by local chieftains, the goðar
quiz.explication: Before 1117, Icelandic law existed only in the lawspeaker's memory: elected for three years by the Lögrétta, he had to recite a third of it each summer at the Lögberg. He did not judge disputes, which fell to the assembly's courts, commanded no expedition, and collected no dues: the Althing had no central administration of that kind.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What ends, in 1117, the purely oral transmission of Icelandic law?
choix: The Althing's decision to have the entire law written down, the following winter
The adoption of Norwegian law after the 1262 union
The death of the last lawspeaker able to recite it
The destruction of the Lögberg in a volcanic eruption
quiz_supplementaire.explication: According to Wikipedia's article on Grágás, the Althing decided in 1117 to set the entire law down in writing; it was drafted the following winter at Hafliði Másson's farm and published in 1118. Norwegian law only arrives after 1262, and neither of the other two answers is documented.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to Wikipedia, why was Grímr Svertingsson's term as lawspeaker cut short?
choix: His voice was too weak to recite the law before the assembly
He was found guilty of distorting a point of law
He refused to appear at the Lögberg for two summers running
The Lögrétta judged him too young for the office
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Wikipedia reports that Grímr Svertingsson had his term cut short because his voice carried poorly for a wholly oral task: reciting the law aloud before the gathered assembly. No wrongdoing or age limit is at issue in the sources.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the Library of Congress blog post, what set the office of lawspeaker apart in the Icelandic Commonwealth?
choix: It was the only paid office in the whole Commonwealth
It was the only office open to people born in Norway
It was a hereditary office, passed from father to son
It was held for life, with no term limit
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Library of Congress blog post states that the lawspeaker was a paid citizen, and that it was the only paid post in the Icelandic Commonwealth. He was elected for three years, not for life, and nothing in the sources points to a hereditary office or one reserved for Norwegians.
